full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M.  Abdul Hakim, J:- This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-9 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 04.10.2003 passed by the Additional District Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No.351 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26.10.1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court No.2, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.248 of 1991. 

2. The opposite party Nos.1-9 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.86 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Bagerhat which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court No.2, Sadar, Bagerhat and renumbered as Title Suit No.248 of 1991 impleading the predecessor of the present petitioners as defendant Nos.1 and 2 praying for declaration of title and partition in respect of 5.79 acres of land as described in schedule to the plaint. 
3. The plaintiff's case, in brief, are that the suit land comprising C.S. Khatian No.14 under Mouza Dhansagar measuring an area of 7.02 acres originally belonged to Tasenuddin Shaikh which was correctly recoded in his name; that Tasenuddin Shaikh died leaving only son Abdul Aziz, daughters, Asiya Khatun and Sona Bibi as widow; that Abdul Aziz died leaving two sons, namely, Ruhul Amin Shaikh and Nazrul Islam Shaikh, three daughters, namely, Raushanara Khatun, Peyara Begum, Zarina Khatun and widow Majeda Khatun; that during his life time Tasenuddin sold .33 acres of land to defendant No.2, Mohabbat Ali Howladar. He further sold 1.82 acres to defendant No.1, Abdul Karim Farazi on 08.04.1953 on condition for re-conveyance. Subsequently, after taking further amount from defendant No.1, relinquish his claims for re-conveyance by a registered deed of Ekrarnama dated 20.03.1964; that Tasenuddin Shaikh said also sold 3.30 acres land to Hasenuddin by two registered deed dated 11.07.1953 and 24.08.1954. He further sold .66 acres to Kashem Ali Farazi and Momen Uddin Hawladar by a registered kabala dated 24.12.1960; that subsequently, Abdul Karim Farazi purchased .66 acres of land from Kashem Ali Farazi and Momenuddin Hawladar. This Abdul Karim Farazi acquired 2.48 acres of land in the suit Jama; that Abdul Karim Farazi, defendant No.1 sold 2.24 acres of land to Tasenuddin Shaikh by a kabala dated 20.03.1964 accordingly Tasenuddin got 3.15 acres of land in the suit Jama but due to inadvertence of the Moharar Dag No.1005 was wrongly inserted in place of Dag No.1075 in the aforesaid kabala dated 20.03.1964. The plaintiffs got their homestead on plot No.1075; that Hasenuddin Hawlader sold 3.30 acres (which he purchased from Tasenuddin Shaikh) to Abdul Aziz, predecessor of the plaintiffs by a kabala deed dated 09.08.1956 and Abdul Aziz sold .66 acres of land to Mahabat Ali Hawladar (defendant No.2). The plaintiff Nos.1-7 have been in possession of the land according to their shares; that plaintiff Nos.8-9 namely, Abdul Hannan Hawladar and Abdul Mannan Hawladar claimed to have purchased .72 acres from Sona Babi, wife of Tasenuddin and thus plaintiffs are entitled to get 5.79 acres of land in suit Jama; that it may be noted here that plaintiff Nos.1-7 filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat, being Title Suit No.40 of 1986 which was renumbered as 379 of 1986 and withdrawn due to some defects; that during recent settlement operation some portion of the shares of plaintiffs have been erroneously recorded in the names of the defendants which is requires to be corrected; that as some of the defendants having been co-sharers in the disputed Jama and some of them being the claimants of shares on vague deed, the co-sharers cannot arrive at a common platform for payment of rent for the same as there was no amicable partition amount the co-sharers and as defendant Nos.l-3 illegally want to retain the jama property in their possession, a partition by metes and bounds among the co-sharers is required with a view to removing all the aforesaid problems. The plaintiffs requested the defendants for partition but they refused to do so on 24th Agrahayan, 1394 B.S. corresponding to 11.12.1987 and hence the suit. 

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the lands of the suit Jama belonged to Tasenuddin Shaikh and he sold 1.82 acres of land to defendant No.1 by a kabala deed dated 08.4.1953 on condition of its re-conveyance on payment of the consideration amount and the defendant No.1 executed an Ekrarnama in favour of (Tasenuddin Shaikh) to that effect. He did not return the consideration amount in pursuance of the condition of the Ekrarnama; that Tasenuddin Shaikh subsequently sold .66 acres of land by a registered deed dated 24.12.1960 to Kasem Farazi and Momenuddin Molla both of whom sold out the same to defendant No.1 by a kabala dated 27.11.1962 and thus defendant No.1 acquired title to 2.48 acres of land of the suit Jama by purchase and he had been in possession of the same since purchase but Nine Annas and Eighteen Gandas equal to 3.89 acres have been recorded in the name of defendant No.1 in the Revisional Survey and the State Acquisition Khatian concerned; that although defendant No.1 did not put any claim over the excess land recorded in his name yet his heirs may claim it in future and although the conditional sale deed executed by Tasenuddin in favour of defendant No.1 became out and out a sale deed for non-compliance of the conditions of the said Ekrarnama yet he did not forego his claim in writing and it may create problems in future and in apprehension of the aforesaid facts and circumstances it was settled between Tasenuddin Shaikh and defendant No.1 that Tasenuddin would execute a deed foregoing his claim of re-conveyance and defendant No.1 would execute another deed to the effect that he would not put any claim over the excess land recorded in his name. Accordingly, two deeds were executed and registered on 20.03.1964 one by Tasenuddin and another by defendant No.1; that Tasenuddin executed `Na-Dabi' deed dated 20.03.1964 foregoing his claim stating that upon peculiar circumstances did not permit him to take back the land measuring 1.82 acres sold to the defendant No.1 on condition of re-conveyance; that Tasenuddin in connivance with the deed writer, identifier and witnesses got a sale deed written in respect of 2.24 acres of land and executed by defendant No.1 giving him an impression that it was a deed of `Na-Dabi' Patta. The deed, in question, was registered by practicing fraud. It was not read over to defendant No. 1. It was a fraudulent deed without any consideration. Tasenuddin did not disclose about it nor did he claim and possess land by virtue of that fraudulent deed. 

5. Defendant No.2 in his written statement stated that Tasenuddin transferred .33 acres of land to this defendant by a registered Patta. After his death, his son Abdul Aziz sold .66 acres of land by a kabala deed dated 22.02.1963. Tasenuddin gave settlement of .40 acres of land to Arab Ali Shaikh who made an oral gift of the same in favour of his son Kadam Ali; defendant No.2 in the name of his son Abdul Hoque Hawladar purchased .14 acres of land from Kadam Ali Shaikh by a registered kahala deed dated 20.05.1957; that Kadam Ali died leaving two wife's namely. Bibijan and Zarina Bibi sold .10 acres of land from Dag No.1067 to defendant No.2 by a kahala deed dated 13.03.1958 and this kabala deed was taken in the name of his son Abdul Jalil Hawladar. The Water and Power Development Board acquired .16 acres of land from co-sharer of Kadam Ali. The plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree as prayed for. 

6. In the suit, plaintiff examined 3 PWs on the other hand defendant examined 4 DWs to prove their respective cases. 

7. The learned Assistant Judge upon hearing and considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 26.10.1992, on the findings that suit is bad for defect of parties and plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their title and possession on the suit land by producing any documents and further failed to produce the kabala dated 20.03.1964. 

8. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No.35I of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Bagerhat. Consequently appeal was transferred to the. Court of Additional District Judge, Bagerhat, who by his judgment and decree dated 04.10.2003 allowed the appeal and decreed the suit and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. 

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment of the appellate Court, the defendants moved this Court in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule. 

10. Mr. Sadananda Rana the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners submits that the suit is bad for defect of parties since in the suit, plaintiffs did not implead the heirs of Kadam Ali and R.S. recorded tenant Arab Ali Shaikh but the appellate Court erroneously found that suit is not bad for defect of parties and decreed the suit. In this connection learned Advocate cited a decision reported in 37 DLR(AD) 216. Learned Advocate further submits that the appellate Court did not at all reverse the findings of the trial Court in respect of the Exhibit-4(F) and plaintiffs failed to produce the original deed in support of their claim. The appellate Court completely failed to appreciate and consider that the documents filed by the plaintiffs in the list of documents dated 10.03.1988 which is not tally with the documents filed by the Firishti dated 30.10.2012. He next submits that the judgment of the appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this respect learned Advocate referred 3 decisions reported in 1 MLR (AD) (1996) 430, 3 BLC (AD) 38 and 55 DLR (AD) 20. He also submits that the appellate Court totally misread and misconstrued the evidence and materials on record and also the judgment of the trial court and accordingly prayed that the rule should be made absolute. Further, in reply to the submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties, Mr. Sadananda Rana, submits that the plaintiffs have ample opportunity to produce/proves their documents in the appellate court but plaintiffs was totally negligent in filing those documents of title. Since sufficient materials and evidence are already on the suit should not sent back on remand as prayed by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. In this respect of the learned Advocate cited two decisions reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74 and 47 DLR (AD) 162. 

11. On the other hand, Mr. A.B.M. Bayezid, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties submits that the plaintiffs claimed their title in 1.82 acres through his father who transferred the said to defendant No.1 dated 08.04.1953 by registered sale deed dated 03.04.1953 coupled with registered Ekrarnama dated 08.04.1953 and confirmed- the sale by registered Ekrarnama dated 20.03.1964. The learned Advocate for the Opposite-parties further submits that certified copy of those documents are filed in court by the list of documents (Firishti) dated 13.10.2012. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties next submits that the plaintiffs exhibited series of documents to prove their title in the suit land by exhibiting C.S. and S.A. Khatian and rents receipts. Thus the plaintiffs were able to prove their title and possession in the suit land. Learned Advocate for the opposite-parties also submits that the judgment of the appellate court is a proper judgment of reversal and the appellate court on consideration materials and evidence on record rightly reversed the decisions of the trial Court, as such same cannot be interfere in the revisional Court. He lastly submits that the appellate court after considering the evidence of DW2 rightly found that suit is not bad for defect of parties. 

12. It appears that the trial Court on consideration of evidence and materials on record clearly found that suit is hard for defect of parties since the heirs of Kadam Ali and R.S. recorded owner Arab Ali Shaikh were not made parties in the present suit. The learned trial court on consideration of Exhibit-3 categorically found that Arab Ali Shaikh was R.S recorded tenant and main party in the present suit and co—share in the suit land but without impleading Arab Ali, the present suit for partition was field. In a partition suit, the established principle of law is that all co-sharer should be impleaded and failure implead any co-sharer render the suit liable for dismissal on the ground of maintainability. In this respect reliance may be place in the case of Mobinnessa and others Vs. Khalilur Rahman and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 216. 

13. It further appears that the trial court specially found that the documents filed by the plaintiffs are all certified copies and those were not marked as exhibits as per Order XIII rule 4(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this respect learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-opposite parties admits that although the documents were filed by the plaintiffs but those were not marked as exhibit. In this connection the learned Advocate for the opposite parties tried to submits since the documents are already on record the plaintiffs may be given chance to prove the same as per law. In reply learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners submits that although the plaintiffs hand an opportunity to produce the said documents in the appellate court but in this respect the plaintiffs did not taken any steps in the appellate Court. So, there is no scope to send back the case on remand to fill up the lacuna of the plaintiffs as it appears apparently that the plaintiffs were extremely negligence in this respect. Moreover, it appears that there is no misreading and non-consideration of any materials evidence on record. Thus there is no scope to send the case back on remand. In this respect of our apex court has already settle the principle that remand as contemplated under Order XLI, Rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not of matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in the any party's pleading. 

14. It transpires that the father of defendant No.1 Abdul Karim Farazi purchased 1.82  acres of suit land from Tasenuddin, the predecessor of the plaintiffs by registered Kabala dated 08.04.1953. Thereafter, Tasenuddin also sold .66 acres of to Kashem Ali Farazi and Momin Uddin Howlader by registered deed dated 24.12.1960 and they sold out the same to defendant no.1 by a registered Kabala dated 27.11.1962. Thus defendant no.1 acquired title in 2.48 acres in the suit Jama by the aforesaid purchases. Subsequently, the plaintiffs claimed that their predecessor, Tasenuddin Shaikh purchased 2.24 acres of suit land from predecessor of the defendant no.1, Abdul Karim by a Kabala dated 20.03.1964 although the plaintiffs predecessor claimed that he purchased the suit land from the predecessor of the defendant no.1 by kabala dated 20.03.1964 but failed to produced neither the certified copy nor the original of the said Kabala. Rather the plaintiff’s field different Kabalas by filling a Frishti which was not tally with the documents filed with the frishti in the suit. 

15. It further appears that in the instant case the specific findings of the trial court have not been reversed by the lower appellate court exercising its power under Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court having considered of the materials on record rightly dismissed the suit with some specific findings which have not been reversed by the court of appeal below which is not a proper judgment of the reversal, appellate court thus committed error of law in reversing the judgment of the trial court. In this connection we can place reliance on the decision in the case of Hajarilal Mondal and others Vs. Md. Mozzaffar Bapari and others reported in 8 BLC (AD) 77, wherein it has been held that it is a settled principle of law that the lower appellate court being the final court of fact will have to discuss and reassess the evidence on record independently while either reversing or affirming the finding of the trial court. In case of reversal it is more incumbent upon the appellate court to reassess the evidence on record and to arrive at his own independent finding. 

16. It has also been well settled by our apex Court, the plaintiff in order to succeed must established the own case to obtained a decree and weakness of the defendant case is no ground in the passing of the decree in favour of the plaintiff. It appears that in the present case plaintiffs did not take any steps to prove their title in the suit land as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get a decree of partition where they failed to prove their title in the possession in the suit land as co-hearer in the suit land. It is further evident from the appellate court judgment that the appellate court without considering the evidence and materials on record abruptly came to a finding that the plaintiffs had right, title and interest in 5.79 acres of land but decreed the suit only for a total area of 1.23 acres out of which plaintiff Nos.1, 2 and 16 will get .24 decimal, .85 decimals and .14 decimals respectively. Thus it is evident from the judgment of the appellate court that whether the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree of for 5.79 acres or 1.23 acres land. Thus it is apparent that the appellate court failed to apply the judicial mind in passing decree in favor of the plaintiffs. 

17. I therefore, find substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. In the aforesaid promises, I set-aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court and restored those of the trial Court. 

18. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. 

19. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated. 

20. Send down the Lower Court Records expeditiously with a copy of judgment for information. 

End.
